                                                      SOLUTION OF THE MUMFORD–SHAH CONJECTURE

                                                                                     FRANCESCO DEANGELIS


                                                  Abstract. We prove the Mumford–Shah conjecture, formulated in 1989, by completing the
                                                  classification of blow-up limits of minimizers in the plane. The remaining case concerns limits
                                                  whose discontinuity set is noncompact and has connected complement. In this setting, we
                                                  rule out bounded connected components using second-variation inequalities obtained from
                                                  combined inner and outer variations associated with two perpendicular translations of a




arXiv:2609.26732v2 [math.AP] 5 Oct 2026
                                                  compact subset separated from the rest of the discontinuity set. Established results then
                                                  imply that the discontinuity set is connected, and the known classification for connected
                                                  discontinuity sets completes the proof.




                                                                          1. Introduction and main result
                                              The Mumford–Shah functional was introduced as a variational model for image segmentation
                                          [MS89]. Its unknowns are a function u, representing a piecewise smooth approximation of a
                                          given image g, and a set K, representing its edges. The model balances the Dirichlet energy
                                          of u away from K, the length of K, and the discrepancy between u and the image. This
                                          competition leads to a free discontinuity problem: both the function and the set across which
                                          it may jump are determined by minimization.
                                              Let Ω ⊂ R2 be open, let g ∈ L∞ (Ω; R), and let λ ≥ 0. For a relatively closed, countably
                                             1                                            1,2
                                          H -rectifiable set K ⊂ Ω and a function u ∈ Wloc    (Ω \ K; R), we consider
                                                                                 Z
                                                                                         |∇u|2 + λ|u − g|2 dx + H1 (K ∩ U )
                                                                                                             
                                                               Eλ (u, K; U ) =                                                                      (1.1)
                                                                                  U \K

                                          for bounded open sets U ⊂ Ω. The term λ U \K |u − g|2 dx is called the fidelity term: it
                                                                                                R

                                          penalizes the discrepancy between u and the prescribed datum g, with weight λ. The Dirichlet
                                          term penalizes large spatial gradients, whereas the length term makes discontinuities costly;
                                          allowing jumps can, however, reduce the cost of approximating sharp transitions in g.
                                             The central regularity question concerns the geometry of the minimizing set K. The
                                          conjecture of Mumford and Shah predicts that, in the interior of the domain, K is a locally
                                          finite union of C 1 arcs, which may have free endpoints and may meet only in triple junctions
                                          with angles of 120◦ . Thus a point of K should have precisely one of three local configurations:
                                          a regular arc, a loose end, or a triple junction. The difficulty is to derive this description from
                                          minimality without assuming in advance that K is connected, has finitely many components, or
                                          already consists of curves. In this paper we prove the planar interior conjecture by completing
                                          the classification of generalized global minimizers.

                                          Background and earlier results. The existence theory rests on formulations that allow
                                          discontinuity sets with no prescribed smoothness. De Giorgi and Ambrosio [DGA88] introduced
                                          the space of special functions of bounded variation, and Ambrosio [Amb90] developed an
                                          existence theory for free discontinuity energies in this setting. The density estimates and
                                          essential closedness theorem of De Giorgi, Carriero and Leaci [DGCL89] link the weak
                                                                                                1
2                                    FRANCESCO DEANGELIS


formulation to minimization over pairs (u, K) with K closed. Dal Maso, Morel and Solimini
[DMMS92] developed a complementary geometric approach to existence and approximation.
These results provide a framework in which the regularity conjecture can be studied without
building its conclusion into the admissible class; see also [AFP].
   A major part of the subsequent theory consists of ε-regularity results: sufficiently good
approximation by an expected model at one scale implies regularity at smaller scales. David
[Dav96] established such results near straight lines and triple junctions. The work of Ambrosio–
Pallara [AP97] and Ambrosio–Fusco–Pallara [AFP97] developed partial regularity in arbitrary
dimension. In particular, the discontinuity set of a planar minimizer is locally a regular arc
at H1 -almost every point. This almost-everywhere description does not by itself control the
exceptional points or exclude the accumulation of small connected components.
   The loose-end case required a further development. Even when the set was known to consist
of a single arc ending at an interior point, the existence of a tangent at that endpoint was
a separate issue. De Lellis, Focardi and Ghinassi [DLFG21] proved an ε-regularity theorem
near the crack-tip model, establishing regularity up to the loose end and vanishing curvature
there; see also the earlier work of Andersson and Mikayelyan [AM19]. The treatment of the
fidelity term, together with a unified account of the planar theory, is given in the monograph
of De Lellis and Focardi [DLF]. Earlier systematic accounts include [Dav05]. Another line of
progress concerns higher integrability: De Lellis and Focardi [DLF13] proved that ∇u belongs
locally to Lp for some p > 2 in the plane, and De Philippis and Figalli [DPF14] established
the corresponding result in arbitrary dimension.
   Further contributions to the regularity theory include higher regularity of the regular part of
the discontinuity set [AFP99], flatness and finiteness results [Leg99], quantitative density lower
bounds [LF13], and monotonicity formulae for more general free discontinuity problems [BL14].
For planar minimizers of the fidelity-free functional, Fischer [Fis22] obtained a monotonicity
formula for the David–Léger entropy truncated at the sharp level 3/2, without a connectedness
assumption on the discontinuity set, and derived an optimal lower bound on the energy density
at points where u is not smooth. In dimension three, regularity near minimal cones [Lem11],
rigidity of global minimizers [Lem15], and stationarity of crack-front configurations [LM18]
have also been investigated. More recently, Zhang [Zha25] gave an alternative proof of a local
square-root growth estimate at tip points, extending an estimate of David and Léger. Labourie
and Lemenant [LL26] proved that a planar minimizer u has at most three distinct limit values
at each point of K, when approached from Ω \ K, answering a question of De Giorgi.
   The connection between local regularity and global geometry comes from blow-up analysis.
The rescaling
                                 K −x
                          Kx,r =        ,     ux,r (y) = r−1/2 u(x + ry)
                                    r
puts the Dirichlet energy and the length on the same scale:
                           E0 (ux,r , Kx,r ; BR ) = r−1 E0 (u, K; BrR (x)).
The fidelity term disappears in the limit as r ↓ 0. Compactness, with suitable normalizations
of the additive constants on different complementary components, leads to generalized global
minimizers of the fidelity-free energy. The expected models are the constant configuration,
the pure jump across a straight line, the triple junction, and the crack tip. The latter consists
of a half-line and a function with square-root growth; its precise normalization is recalled in
(2.2). The compactness and ε-regularity theory makes the interior conjecture equivalent to the
assertion that these models exhaust the generalized global minimizers [DLF, Theorem 1.4.5].
                        SOLUTION OF THE MUMFORD–SHAH CONJECTURE                                  3


   Several fundamental classification results establish this assertion under additional geometric
hypotheses. Bonnet [Bon96] introduced a monotonicity argument and classified global mini-
mizers whose discontinuity set is connected. Bonnet and David [BD01] proved that the crack
tip is globally minimizing and obtained a stronger rigidity theorem, which applies when all but
at most one connected component of K are contained in a common compact set. David and
Léger [DL02] classified the case in which K disconnects the plane, leaving only the straight line
and the triple junction, and showed that K has at most one unbounded connected component.
The forms of these results used below are recalled in Section 2. Together they isolate the
remaining difficulty in configurations with disconnected K and connected complement, for
which bounded components cannot all be confined to one compact set.
   There is also a related regularity problem at the boundary of the ambient domain. For
prescribed Dirichlet data, the author [Dea24] studied boundary blow-ups and proved an
ε-regularity theorem near the tangent line to the boundary. The result proved here concerns
interior points; the boundary problem involves a different class of limiting minimizers.
Main result. We now specify the local minimality convention in the statement. We call
(u, K) admissible if its energy is locally finite, that is, Eλ (u, K; U ) < ∞ for every open U ⋐ Ω.
We call an admissible pair (u, K) an absolute minimizer if, for every bounded open U ⊂ Ω,
                                     Eλ (u, K; U ) ≤ Eλ (v, L; U )
for every admissible (v, L) for which some compact C ⊂ U satisfies
                     L \ C = K \ C,           v=u          a.e. on Ω \ (C ∪ K ∪ L).          (1.2)
This is absolute minimality in [DLF, Section 1.1 and Definition 1.2.1]; competitor sets L are
rectifiable, but there is no restriction on their topology. We call K reduced if
                    H1 (K ∩ Br (x)) > 0        whenever x ∈ K and Br (x) ⊂ Ω.                (1.3)
When Ω = R2 , the same definition is used in every ball. This condition requires K to coincide
locally with the support of its length measure, excluding extraneous points that would obscure
a geometric statement.
Theorem 1.1 (Planar interior regularity). Let (u, K) be an absolute minimizer of (1.1), and
suppose that K is reduced. For every x ∈ K there are r > 0 with Br (x) ⊂ Ω, an integer
m ∈ {1, 2, 3}, positive numbers ℓ1 , . . . , ℓm , and injective maps
                              γi ∈ C 1 ([0, ℓi ]; R2 ),        i = 1, . . . , m,
with
                            |γi′ (s)| = 1   (0 ≤ s ≤ ℓi ),            γi (0) = x,            (1.4)
                            γi (ℓi ) ∈ ∂Br (x),           γi ([0, ℓi )) ⊂ Br (x),
                                                          m
                                                          [
                                    K ∩ Br (x) =             γi ([0, ℓi ]),                  (1.5)
                                                      i=1
                            γi ([0, ℓi ]) ∩ γj ([0, ℓj ]) = {x}          (i ̸= j).
Endpoint derivatives are one-sided. The outward unit tangents τi = γi′ (0) satisfy
                                                         1
                   τ1 + τ2 = 0 (m = 2),      τi · τj = −    (i ̸= j, m = 3).                 (1.6)
                                                         2
The set of points with m = 1 or m = 3 is locally finite in Ω.

Outline of the proof. The proof reduces to the classification of reduced generalized global
minimizers. By the established results recalled above, it remains to consider noncompact
K with connected complement R2 \ K. Our strategy is to use second variations to exclude
bounded connected components of K. Indeed, the David–Léger theorem gives at most one
unbounded component; once every component is unbounded, K is connected and the known
classification applies.
   A bounded connected component need not be isolated from the other components, so it
cannot necessarily be translated independently. However, Lemma 3.3 shows that it is contained
in a nonempty compact subset S ⊂ K which is both open and closed relative to K. Since K is
noncompact, S is a proper subset of K. Moreover, compactness of S and closedness of K \ S
imply that the two sets have positive distance. We can therefore translate S while keeping the
rest of K fixed, preserving its length. Proposition 3.1 rules out such a set by combining the
second-variation inequalities for two perpendicular translations, while allowing u to adjust to
each deformation.
   Our starting point, Lemma 3.2, is a second-variation estimate for a generalized global
minimizer with connected complement D = R2 \ K, valid for every deformation field X ∈
Cc∞ (R2 ; R2 ). No smoothness of K in the region affected by the deformation is required. We
consider the combined inner and outer variations
                    Φt = Id +tX,          Kt = Φt (K),        ut ◦ Φt = u + tφ,
where φ ∈ TK and
           TK = {φ ∈ W 1,2 (D) : φ = 0 a.e. outside some compact subset of R2 }.
The coefficient of t2 in the energy expansion is
                                   QX + ∥∇φ∥22 + 2⟨mX , ∇φ⟩.
Here QX is the coefficient for the pure inner variation, obtained by setting φ = 0, while mX
couples the deformation to the correction of u through the inner product ⟨mX , ∇φ⟩ above.
Explicitly,
                        mX = (div X)I − DX − (DX)T ∇u,
                                                               
                               Z
                                     |(DX)T ∇u|2 − det(DX)|∇u|2 dx
                                                                       
                        QX =
                                D
                                 1
                                     Z
                                           |DX τ |2 − (τ · DX τ )2 dH1 ,
                                                                   
                               +
                                 2    K

where τ is a unit approximate tangent to K. Norms and inner products are taken in L2 (R2 ; R2 ).
   For each fixed X, inner variations alone give QX ≥ 0. The freedom to choose φ gives a
stronger condition: completing the square and taking the infimum over φ ∈ TK yields
                                          QX ≥ ∥ΠK mX ∥22 ,
where ΠK is the orthogonal projection onto the L2 closure of the gradients of functions in TK .
Thus the optimization quantifies how much the quadratic cost of a prescribed deformation
can be reduced by adjusting u.
   Second variations of the Mumford–Shah functional were also studied by Cagnetti, Mora
and Morini [CMM08]. Their analysis concerns deformations supported in the regular part
of the discontinuity set, with the function chosen to minimize the Dirichlet energy on the
deformed domain with fixed boundary values.
                       SOLUTION OF THE MUMFORD–SHAH CONJECTURE                                 5


   We then apply this general estimate to X1 = χe1 and X2 = χe2 , where χ is a smooth
compactly supported cutoff equal to one near S and zero near K \ S. These fields generate
the two perpendicular translations of S. Their pure inner quadratic costs QX1 and QX2 are
already nonnegative, so the essential information comes from the projection term obtained
by optimizing over φ. The associated fields mX1 and mX2 are related by a 90◦ rotation and
satisfy
                             QX1 + QX2 = ∥mX1 ∥22 = ∥mX2 ∥22 .
Let Π denote the orthogonal projection onto the L2 closure of the gradients of functions in
Cc∞ (R2 ). The Hodge decomposition on R2 gives
                             ∥ΠmX1 ∥22 + ∥ΠmX2 ∥22 = QX1 + QX2 .
Since the restrictions to D of functions in Cc∞ (R2 ) belong to TK , the space defining Π is
contained in the space defining ΠK . Thus replacing Π by ΠK can only increase each squared
norm. On the other hand, the second-variation inequalities bound ∥ΠK mXi ∥22 by QXi for
i = 1, 2. Summing these inequalities forces equality throughout. Let v be a real scalar potential
such that
                                           ∇v = ΠmX1 .
It satisfies ∆v = div mX1 , so it is harmonic near K, where mX1 = 0. The equality conditions
imply that both the normal and tangential derivatives of v vanish along every regular arc of
K. Thus ∇v = 0 on these arcs.
   To connect this information back to u, we use the equation for the potential to split one
derivative of u into two harmonic functions. One extends through S and the other through
K \ S. The vanishing conditions and unique continuation make both functions constant. It
follows that ∇u is constant, and the linear energy-growth bound forces it to vanish. The
classification of minimizers with vanishing Dirichlet energy then contradicts the presence of S.
   This excludes bounded connected components in the remaining case and completes the
classification in Theorem 3.4. The planar regularity statement, Theorem 1.1, then follows by
the existing compactness and regularity theory, including regularity at loose ends.
   Section 2 records the precise results from that theory needed for this implication. Section 3
proves compact translation rigidity and its topological consequence, and completes the global
classification.

                       2. Reduction to a global classification
   All references to the established theory below use the published monograph [DLF].
   We use generalized global minimizer exactly as in [DLF, Definition 2.2.4]: it is a triple
(u, K, {pkl }) arising from rescaled absolute minimizers. The extended-real parameters pkl
record relative additive constants on the connected components of R2 \ K. They are part of
the definition; when R2 \ K is connected, the only parameter is p11 = 0.
   The compactness theorem below requires a uniform L∞ bound on the minimizers before
rescaling [DLF, Assumption 2.2.1(iv)]. For blow-ups of a fixed absolute minimizer (u, K) at
an interior point, we obtain this bound by working on a sufficiently small ball. The maximum
principle [DLF, Lemma 2.1.1] gives local boundedness of u when λ > 0. When λ = 0, a local
truncation gives a bounded function u   e such that (u
                                                     e, K) is still an absolute minimizer and
∇ue = ∇u. We apply the compactness theorem to this bounded minimizer.
   The compactness theorem [DLF, Theorem 2.2.3] supplies a generalized global limit
(u, K, {pkl }) along a subsequence of every sequence of interior rescalings. It gives local
6                                        FRANCESCO DEANGELIS


Hausdorff convergence to K and separate convergence of Dirichlet energies and length
measures. The limiting set K is reduced, countably H1 -rectifiable, and locally of finite length,
while u ∈ W 1,2 (BR \ K) for every R > 0. For every generalized global minimizer (u, K, {pkl }),
the upper density bound [DLF, Lemma 2.1.2] gives
                Z
                             |∇u|2 + H1 (K ∩ BR (z)) ≤ 2πR       (z ∈ R2 , R > 0).             (2.1)
                  BR (z)\K

Moreover, [DLF, Corollary 3.1.5] gives a relatively open subset of regular points of K of full
H1 measure. At each such point x, there is r > 0 such that K ∩ Br (x) is a single embedded
C 1 arc.
   If D = R2 \ K is connected, the exterior separation condition on competitors in [DLF,
Definition 2.2.2] is vacuous. Consequently [DLF, Theorem 2.2.3(ii)] makes (u, K) an ordinary
absolute minimizer of the fidelity-free energy on the plane. In particular, the compactly
supported combined inner and outer variations used in Section 3 are admissible.
   A generalized global minimizer (u, K, {pkl }) is called elementary if ∇u = 0 almost everywhere
on R2 \ K. By [DLF, Theorem 2.4.1], in this case K is either empty, a straight line (the
pure-jump model), or the union of three half-lines with a common endpoint and pairwise
angles of 120◦ (the triple-junction model). In each case, u is constant on every connected
component of R2 \ K. The other canonical model is the crack tip. Up to translation, rotation,
sign, and an additive constant, its set K and function u are given by
                                         K = {(r, 0) : r ≥ 0},
                                        2√                                                     (2.2)
                                     r
                                                 θ
                         u(r, θ) =          r cos , r > 0, 0 < θ < 2π.
                                        π        2
The parameters pkl in the two disconnected models are interpreted as in [DLF, Section 2.4].
For a generalized global minimizer (u, K, {pkl }), we shall use the following classification results:
     (i) If R2 \ K is disconnected, then ∇u = 0 almost everywhere on R2 \ K, and K is either a
         straight line or the triple-junction configuration described above [DLF, Theorem 4.4.1].
    (ii) K has at most one unbounded connected component [DLF, Corollary 4.4.3].
   (iii) If all but at most one connected component of K lie in one common compact set,
         then the minimizer is elementary or (u, K) is the canonical crack tip (2.2), up to the
         transformations specified above [DLF, Theorem 1.4.6, first paragraph].
These are the established David–Léger and Bonnet–David classification results, in the form
needed for generalized limits.
   By [DLF, Theorem 1.4.5], it suffices to prove the classification stated in Theorem 3.4. After
the usual local normalization and rescaling, the regularity theorem [DLF, Theorem 1.3.3] gives
Theorem 1.1. Along each sufficiently short C 1 branch issuing from x, the distance from x
increases strictly. We may therefore choose a smaller ball whose boundary meets each branch
exactly once. Parametrizing the resulting closed arcs by arclength gives (1.4)–(1.5). The local
description at every point of K also gives a neighborhood containing no endpoints or triple
junctions other than, possibly, that point itself. Since K is relatively closed in Ω, such points
cannot accumulate in Ω and are therefore locally finite.

                 3. Compact translations and global classification
   We first prove the compact translation rigidity result and then use it to complete the
classification of generalized global minimizers.
                        SOLUTION OF THE MUMFORD–SHAH CONJECTURE                                      7


3.1. Admissible variations and optimization over corrections. For a closed set K ⊂ R2
of zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure, put D = R2 \ K and define the real test space
           TK = {φ ∈ W 1,2 (D) : φ = 0 a.e. outside some compact subset of R2 }.
We shall use the closed subspace
                                                             L2 (R2 ;R2 )
                                VK = {∇φ : φ ∈ TK }
and its orthogonal projection ΠK . Sets of zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure are ignored
when identifying vector fields on D with vector fields on the plane.
  Let (u, K, {pkl }) be a generalized global minimizer with R2 \ K connected. Absolute
minimality gives the weak equation
                                Z

and the inner variation identity

Here X ∈ Cc∞ (R2 ; R2 ) and τ is a unit approximate tangent to K. These are the usual
variational identities; see [DLF, Section 2.5]. Minimality also gives second-order stability
under the combined inner and outer variations
                      Φt = Id +tX,           Kt = Φt (K),        ut ◦ Φt = u + tφ.                (3.3)
These reduce to inner variations when φ = 0 and to outer variations when X = 0. Differences
of the infinite global energies are evaluated on a bounded region containing the support of the
variation.
Proposition 3.1 (Compact translation rigidity). Let (u, K, {pkl }) be a reduced generalized
global minimizer with R2 \ K connected. There is no nonempty compact proper subset of K
which is both open and closed relative to K.
Lemma 3.2 (Second variation optimized over corrections to u). Let (u, K, {pkl }) be a gener-

Proof. Fix φ ∈ TK , and choose a ball B containing the supports of X and φ compactly. For
sufficiently small |t|, the map Φt in (3.3) is a diffeomorphism equal to the identity outside a
compact subset of B; in particular, Φt (B) = B. For the matrix calculation, write A = DX.

Since DX is bounded and |τ | = 1, the O(t3 ) remainder estimates in the expansions of Mt
and the tangential Jacobian are uniform in the spatial variable. Since u and φ have finite
Dirichlet energy on B \ K and H1 (K ∩ B) < ∞, the integrated remainder is o(t2 ) for each
fixed φ. Since the competitors are admissible for both signs of sufficiently small t, minimality
implies that the differentiable function t 7→ E0 (ut , Kt ; B) has a local minimum at t = 0. Thus
its linear coefficient vanishes, and the preceding expansions give

where norms and inner products are in L2 (R2 ; R2 ). Dividing the minimality inequality by t2

  Since ∇φ ∈ VK , orthogonal projection gives ⟨mX , ∇φ⟩ = ⟨ΠK mX , ∇φ⟩. Completing the
square,
                    ∥∇φ∥22 + 2⟨mX , ∇φ⟩ = ∥∇φ + ΠK mX ∥22 − ∥ΠK mX ∥22 .
By the definition of VK , there are φj ∈ TK such that ∇φj → −ΠK mX in L2 (R2 ; R2 ). Applying
the preceding inequality to φj and passing to the limit proves (3.6). The limit t → 0 is taken
first for each fixed test, so no remainder estimate uniform in j is needed. In particular, the
projected field need not itself be the gradient of an element of TK .                       □

3.2. Two translations and the Hodge decomposition.
Proof of Proposition 3.1. Suppose that S ⊊ K is nonempty, compact and relatively open and
closed. Its nonempty complement K \ S is closed and has positive distance from S. We may
therefore choose a real χ ∈ Cc∞ (R2 ) such that
                            χ=1      near S,        χ=0       near K \ S.
Thus supp ∇χ is a compact subset of D. Reducedness and relative openness imply
                                          0 < H1 (S) < ∞.                                    (3.7)
   Set X1 = χe1 and X2 = χe2 . The corresponding deformations translate S rigidly and are
the identity in a neighborhood of K \ S. Let J(a, b) = (−b, a). Substituting into (3.4)–(3.5)
gives
                       m := mX1 = (−χx ux − χy uy , −χy ux + χx uy ),
                             mX2 = Jm,                                                       (3.8)
                                      Z                             Z
                             QX1 =        u2x |∇χ|2 ,      QX2 =        u2y |∇χ|2 .
                                      D                             D
Consequently
                                     QX1 + QX2 = ∥m∥22 .                                      (3.9)
The field m is smooth and compactly supported in D, since (3.1) makes u harmonic there.
  Let V be the L2 closure of gradients of real functions in Cc∞ (R2 ), and let Π be its orthogonal
projection. Then V ⊂ VK . The planar L2 Helmholtz–Hodge decomposition (see [Gal11,
Section III.1]) gives
                                   L2 (R2 ; R2 ) = V ⊕⊥ JV.
Write
                                  m = g + Jh,        g, h ∈ V.
                                    2        2
Since V and JV are orthogonal in L and J = −I, we have
                            Πm = g,         Π(Jm) = Π(Jg − h) = −h.
Therefore, using that J preserves the L2 norm,
                              ∥Πm∥22 + ∥Π(Jm)∥22 = ∥g∥22 + ∥h∥22
                                                        = ∥g∥22 + ∥Jh∥22                    (3.10)
                                                        = ∥m∥22 .
Since V ⊂ VK , for every f ∈ L2 (R2 ; R2 ) we have ΠK f − Πf ⊥ V, and hence
                            ∥ΠK f ∥22 − ∥Πf ∥22 = ∥ΠK f − Πf ∥22 ≥ 0.
Combining (3.6), (3.9) and (3.10), we obtain
                             ∥m∥22 ≥ ∥ΠK m∥22 + ∥ΠK (Jm)∥22
                                    ≥ ∥Πm∥22 + ∥Π(Jm)∥22 = ∥m∥22 .
The first and last quantities coincide, so equality holds throughout. Using the preceding
projection identity, we obtain
                          ∥ΠK m − Πm∥22 + ∥ΠK (Jm) − Π(Jm)∥22 = 0.
10                                     FRANCESCO DEANGELIS


Both terms are nonnegative, so
                             ΠK m = Πm,               ΠK (Jm) = Π(Jm).
Since f − ΠK f ⊥ VK for every f , we conclude that
                     R1 = m − Πm ⊥ VK ,                   R2 = Jm − Π(Jm) ⊥ VK .            (3.11)
A real scalar potential and the normal conditions. Since Πm ∈ V, it is an L2 limit of gradients
of smooth, compactly supported functions, and hence curl(Πm) = 0 in D′ (R2 ). As the plane
                                                                         1,2
is simply connected, the Poincaré lemma supplies a real function v ∈ Wloc    (R2 ) such that
                            ∇v = Πm,              ∆v = div m         in D′ (R2 ).           (3.12)
The second identity follows because m − Πm is orthogonal to all compactly supported smooth
gradients. Since m ∈ Cc∞ (D; R2 ), elliptic regularity gives v ∈ C ∞ (R2 ), and v is harmonic on a
neighborhood of K.
  Using the decomposition above, (3.11) and (3.12) give
                           R1 = m − ∇v = Jh,                  R2 = Jg = J∇v.
In particular, both residuals are smooth and divergence-free on the plane, and, near K, where
m = 0,
                                   R1 = −∇v,      R2 = J∇v.                               (3.13)
   Fix a regular point of K and choose, in suitable coordinates, a sufficiently small rectangle
U around it such that Γ := K ∩ U is a single C 1 graph. The set U \ K is the union of two
Lipschitz domains U + and U − lying on either side of Γ. Let ν denote the outward unit normal
to U + . For any real η ∈ Cc∞ (U ), define on D
                                              (
                                                  η(x),    x ∈ U +,
                                     φ(x) =
                                                  0,       x ∈ D \ U +.
Since η vanishes near ∂U , this definition creates no jump inside D: the only possible jump
lies on Γ ⊂ K. Thus φ ∈ W 1,2 (D), with ∇φ = 1U + ∇η almost everywhere on D. Its support
in the plane is contained in supp η ⋐ U , so φ ∈ TK .
   Using (3.11) and integration by parts on U + , we obtain, for j = 1, 2,
                                 Z                        Z
                           0=         Rj · ∇φ dx =                Rj · ∇η dx
                                                           U+
                                 ZD                           Z
                             =          η Rj · ν dH1 −               η div Rj dx
                                 ∂U +                           U+
                                 Z
                             = η Rj · ν dH1 .
                             Γ
Here the boundary term on ∂U + \ Γ vanishes because η is supported compactly in U , and the
volume term vanishes because div Rj = 0. Since the identity holds for every η ∈ Cc∞ (U ) and
Rj · ν is continuous on Γ, we conclude that
                                      R1 · ν = R2 · ν = 0           on Γ.
By (3.13),
                                 ∇v · ν = (J∇v) · ν = 0.
The vectors ν and Jν span the plane, so
                            ∇v = 0       on every regular subarc of K.                      (3.14)
                       SOLUTION OF THE MUMFORD–SHAH CONJECTURE                               11


Harmonic separation of the compact piece. We use the following standard harmonic uniqueness
fact: if w is harmonic on a connected open set U ⊂ R2 and ∇w = 0 along a nontrivial
embedded C 1 arc contained in U , then w is constant. Indeed, w = c and ∂ν w = 0 on a
connected subarc. Extending w − c from one side by zero to the other gives a weakly harmonic
function in a small neighborhood, by integration by parts. Interior elliptic regularity and the
identity principle imply that this extension vanishes. Thus w = c on an open subset of U , and
hence throughout U .
   Using uyy = −uxx and uxy = uyx in (3.8), we compute on D
                        div m = −(∆χ)ux − 2∇χ · ∇ux = −∆(χux ).                          (3.15)
Here ux is harmonic on D. By (3.12) and (3.15), the real scalar functions
                            f0 = (1 − χ)ux − v,       f1 = χux + v                       (3.16)
are harmonic on D and satisfy f0 + f1 = ux . Near S, the first equals −v, so it extends
harmonically through S. Near K \ S, the second equals v, so it extends harmonically through
K \ S. Their respective domains of extension are
                            U0 = R2 \ (K \ S),       U1 = R2 \ S.
Both domains are connected: each contains connected D, and every open component meets D
because K has zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
  By (3.7) and full-measure regularity, S contains a regular subarc. Near that subarc f0 = −v,
and (3.14) gives ∇f0 = 0 there. The harmonic uniqueness fact therefore makes f0 constant
throughout U0 . The nonempty relatively open set K \ S also contains a positive-length regular
subarc, by reducedness and full-measure regularity. Near it f1 = v, so the same argument
makes f1 constant throughout U1 .
  It follows that ux = f0 + f1 is constant on D. Harmonicity gives
                              ∇uy = (uxy , uyy ) = (0, −uxx ) = 0.
Connectedness of D then makes uy constant as well. Thus ∇u is a constant vector on D.
Since K has zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure, a nonzero constant gradient would
give quadratic bulk-energy growth, contrary to (2.1). Consequently ∇u = 0 on D. By the
classification of elementary generalized global minimizers [DLF, Theorem 2.4.1], connectedness
of D implies K = ∅, contradicting ∅ ̸= S ⊂ K. This proves the proposition.                  □
3.3. Topological consequence and classification.
Lemma 3.3. Let K ⊂ R2 be closed. If K has no nonempty compact subset that is both
relatively open and relatively closed in K, then every connected component of K is unbounded.
Proof. Suppose that C is a bounded connected component of K. Since C is closed in K and
K is closed in R2 , the set C is closed and bounded in R2 , hence compact. Choose R with
C ⊂ BR and set
                              X := K ∩ B R ,     E := X ∩ ∂BR .
The space X is compact, and C ∩ E = ∅. Moreover, C is a connected component of X: it is
connected and contained in X, and any connected subset of X strictly containing C would
also be a connected subset of K, contradicting the maximality of C.
   We use the standard fact [Eng89, Theorem 6.1.23] that a component of a compact Hausdorff
space is the intersection of all subsets containing it that are both open and closed in that
space. Thus, for each y ∈ E, there is a set Vy ⊂ X, open and closed in X, such that C ⊂ Vy
12                                      FRANCESCO DEANGELIS


and y ∈
      / Vy . The sets X \ Vy form an open cover of E relative to X. Since E is compact, we
can choose finitely many y1 , . . . , yN ∈ E such that
                                       N
                                       [                           N
                                                                   \
                                E⊂          (X \ Vyi ),    W :=          V yi .
                                      i=1                          i=1
Then W is open and closed in X and contains C. The covering property gives W ∩ E = ∅, so
W ⊂ BR . If E = ∅, take W = X, which has the same properties.
   Since W is closed in the compact space X, it is compact and hence closed in R2 , so it is also
relatively closed in K. Since W is open in X, write W = O ∩ X for some open set O ⊂ R2 .
As W ⊂ BR , we have
                                     W = K ∩ (O ∩ BR ),
so W is relatively open in K. Finally, W is nonempty because it contains C. Thus W is
a nonempty compact subset of K that is both relatively open and relatively closed in K,
contrary to the hypothesis.                                                                    □
Theorem 3.4 (Classification of generalized global minimizers).
Let (u, K, {pkl }) be a reduced generalized global minimizer in R2 . Then either ∇u = 0 a.e. on
R2 \ K, so that the minimizer is elementary, or (u, K) is the canonical crack tip (2.2), up to
translation, rotation, sign, and an additive constant.
Proof. Let (u, K, {pkl }) be a generalized global minimizer in the sense of [DLF, Definition 2.2.4].
If R2 \ K is disconnected, [DLF, Theorem 4.4.1] gives a pure-jump or triple-junction model. If
K is compact, including K = ∅, [DLF, Theorem 1.4.6, first paragraph] already applies, since
all components are contained in a common compact set. Its only model with compact K is
the constant minimizer.
   It remains to consider noncompact K with connected complement. Proposition 3.1 excludes
every nonempty compact relatively open-and-closed subset of K, since any such subset
would be proper. Lemma 3.3 therefore makes every component of K unbounded. By [DLF,
Corollary 4.4.3] there is at most one such component, so K is connected. The classification of
generalized global minimizers with connected K [DLF, Theorem 1.4.6] gives the conclusion. □
